opus-5.5.text:
You know, I think one of the most interesting shifts I'm seeing is that AI coding tools have made software engineering dramatically faster. With agentic coding assistants, a small team can now build a prototype in a day or a weekend that might have taken weeks or months before. And when engineering speeds up that much, the bottleneck moves. Increasingly, the bottleneck is product management: deciding what to build.

Traditionally, many teams had something like one product manager for every four to eight engineers. I'm now seeing some teams talk about flipping that ratio, maybe one PM to two engineers, or even one-to-one, because engineers can implement so quickly that the hard part becomes figuring out what users actually want.

So can AI accelerate product management itself? I think yes, but more slowly and unevenly than coding so far. There are clear wins. You can use LLMs to synthesize user interviews, draft specs, brainstorm features, analyze survey data, and even simulate user personas to get a rough first read on an idea. Those are useful. But a lot of good product management still rests on deep empathy with the user, gut instinct built from many conversations, and the judgment to make a quick decision with incomplete data. AI tools help, but they don't yet replace that.

One pattern I like is this: a strong PM, or an engineer with good product instincts, builds an intuitive mental model of the user. That lets them make decisions very fast, often in minutes. When they're unsure, they go get data, whether that's talking to users, running A/B tests, or showing a prototype to people. Then they update their gut. AI can speed up the data-gathering and feedback part of that loop considerably. You can get prototypes in front of users faster, analyze feedback faster, and iterate faster.

So my view is that AI is already a meaningful accelerant for product work, and that the people who'll be most valuable are those who combine technical skill with product sense. I'm seeing more engineers learn to do product work and more PMs learn to code with AI assistance. That blending of roles is one of the most exciting things happening right now.

r002.rationale: It says engineering speeds up, “the bottleneck moves” to product management and deciding what to build.

r003.rationale: It mentions synthesizing user interviews, but does not identify computers interviewing humans at scale as a broadly applicable capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's one of the most underappreciated shifts happening right now. For a long time the bottleneck in building software was engineering. You'd have a product manager who could write a spec, and then it would take weeks or months of engineering time to actually see whether the idea was any good. So PMs learned to be very careful about what they asked for, because every request was expensive.

What's changed is that the cost of writing code has collapsed. With AI coding tools, a competent engineer, or increasingly a PM who knows just a bit of code, can go from an idea to a working prototype in an afternoon instead of a month. And that completely changes the economics of product work. Instead of debating for two weeks whether users would want a feature, you build three versions and put them in front of people.

So the thing I tell teams is that the bottleneck has moved. It used to be engineering capacity. Now it's increasingly product judgment: figuring out what to build, talking to users, deciding what matters. And frankly a lot of companies have the wrong ratio. The old rule of thumb might have been six or seven engineers per PM. I think that ratio is shifting, and in some teams I've seen it move toward something closer to one to one, or even having more PMs than engineers, because getting the product decisions right is now where the leverage is.

The other piece is that PMs themselves can use these tools directly. I've been encouraging everyone, including people who don't think of themselves as technical, to learn to code a little, not to become software engineers, but because being able to tell a computer exactly what you want is a superpower. A PM who can whip up a quick mockup or a data analysis themselves, without waiting in a queue, iterates much faster. And speed of iteration is, in my experience, the single best predictor of whether a team ends up building something people actually want.

So I'm quite optimistic. It's not that PMs get replaced. It's that the job gets more interesting, because the slow, expensive parts of testing an idea are going away, and what's left is the part that really requires taste and understanding of users.

r002.rationale: It says the bottleneck has shifted from engineering capacity to product judgment as coding becomes cheaper, making product decisions more consequential.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a huge opportunity. As AI makes it faster to build software, figuring out what to build becomes even more important. You still need to understand the customer, identify a problem worth solving, and decide whether your solution actually helps.

AI can accelerate a lot of that work. It can help synthesize customer interviews, explore different product concepts, and turn an idea into a prototype that you can put in front of a user. That shortens the loop between having a hypothesis and getting feedback.

But I think the deeper change is that product management becomes more experimental. Instead of spending weeks debating a specification, a team can build a few versions and learn from how people use them. The judgment still matters—especially deciding what evidence to trust—but the cost of testing an idea gets much lower.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a huge opportunity. As AI makes it faster and cheaper to build software, figuring out what to build becomes even more important. You can generate code quickly, but if you’re solving the wrong customer problem, that doesn’t create much value.

AI tools can help product managers synthesize customer interviews, explore requirements, and build prototypes. What excites me most is shortening the loop between an idea and feedback from a user. Instead of writing a document and waiting weeks to see something working, you can get a rough version in front of someone much sooner.

But I would distinguish accelerating the tasks of product management from automating the judgment. Understanding what someone actually needs, deciding which tradeoffs to make, and knowing whether a product is useful still require close contact with users. I think the strongest product managers will use AI to test more ideas and learn faster.
